--- title: "From one participant to a group" --- [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/crossley/eeg_tutorial/blob/main/notebooks/09-group.ipynb) Everything so far has been one participant. That is the right way to learn the methods, but it is not how results are established. One person's brain, on one day, can show almost anything. A finding is something that holds across people. This page takes the two ERP effects from chapter 4, stripe width and feedback, and asks whether they hold in a group of ten participants who did the same task. ## The data For each participant we have the same averages you made in chapter 4, from their first visit: the response to stimuli with wide stripes and with narrow stripes, and the response to correct and incorrect feedback. All the cleaning and averaging has been done, exactly as in chapters 3 and 4, so each file is small. ::: {#7e7f6ca0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path import mne data = Path("data/eeg_tutorial_data_v1") files = sorted((data / "group").glob("*_visit-1-ave.fif")) print(len(files), "participants") wide = [mne.read_evokeds(file, condition="wide") for file in files] narrow = [mne.read_evokeds(file, condition="narrow") for file in files] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 10 participants ``` ::: ::: `wide` is now a list of ten ERPs, one per participant, and so is `narrow`. ## People differ Here is the response to wide stripes at `Oz` for each participant separately. ::: {#13ba4304 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} each = {f"participant {number}": erp for number, erp in enumerate(wide, start=1)} mne.viz.plot_compare_evokeds(each, picks="Oz"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](09-group_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=779 height=587} ::: ::: They all show a response beginning at about 0.1 seconds, but its size, its exact timing and even its shape vary a good deal from person to person. Skulls differ in thickness, the folds of the cortex differ, and people differ in how they do the task. The participant you have been working with (number 1) is just one of these lines. So a difference between two conditions in one participant leaves a question open: is this how brains respond, or how this brain responds? ## The group average Give `plot_compare_evokeds` the two lists and it averages over participants and draws a band around each line. The band shows how much the participants vary: a narrow band means they agree. ::: {#1dfb993a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} mne.viz.plot_compare_evokeds({"wide": wide, "narrow": narrow}, picks="Oz"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](09-group_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=779 height=587} ::: ::: The difference at 0.1 seconds that we saw in one participant is there in the group average too: the line for narrow stripes dips while the line for wide stripes climbs. The bands overlap a great deal, though. That is because they show how much people differ from *each other*, which we have just seen is a lot. They do not show what we care about: whether, *within* each person, wide and narrow differ in the same direction. For that we need each participant's own difference. ## One number per participant A picture is not a test. The usual next step is to reduce each participant to one number per condition, and compare those. A common choice is the **mean amplitude**: the average voltage at a chosen electrode over a chosen stretch of time. We take `Oz` between 0.08 and 0.13 seconds, the first visual response. ::: {#1a6bae73 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd def mean_amplitude(erp, channel, start, end): return erp.copy().pick(channel).crop(start, end).data.mean() * 1e6 table = pd.DataFrame({"wide": [mean_amplitude(erp, "Oz", 0.08, 0.13) for erp in wide], "narrow": [mean_amplitude(erp, "Oz", 0.08, 0.13) for erp in narrow]}) table["difference"] = table["wide"] - table["narrow"] table.round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
wide narrow difference
0 2.6 -2.0 4.6
1 1.2 -3.0 4.1
2 1.9 1.4 0.5
3 2.3 0.6 1.7
4 4.7 2.3 2.3
5 5.7 0.4 5.3
6 -1.5 -3.2 1.7
7 7.1 4.5 2.7
8 8.9 9.3 -0.4
9 6.4 6.2 0.2
``` ::: ::: Each row is a participant, in microvolts. Look down the `difference` column. It is positive for nine of the ten: nearly everyone shows a more positive response to wide stripes, though the size ranges from almost nothing to more than five microvolts. That consistency is the evidence. The standard way to put a number on it is a **paired t-test**, which asks whether the average difference is large compared with how much the differences vary from person to person. ::: {#3b033284 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scipy import stats result = stats.ttest_rel(table["wide"], table["narrow"]) print("t =", round(result.statistic, 2), " p =", round(result.pvalue, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` t = 3.76 p = 0.0045 ``` ::: ::: The **p-value** is the number to read first. Roughly, it is how often a difference this consistent would turn up if stripe width in fact made no difference. Here it is less than one in a hundred, well under the conventional threshold of 0.05. The effect of stripe width on the early visual response holds across the group. Notice what the unit of evidence was. Each participant had about two hundred trials in each average, but they contributed *one number* each. The test has ten data points, not thousands. More trials make each participant's number more precise; only more participants tell you whether the effect is general [@boudewyn2018]. ## The feedback effect Now the same for the feedback-related negativity. In chapter 4 we looked at `FCz` between about 0.2 and 0.35 seconds, expecting the response to incorrect feedback to be more negative. ::: {#e8e251cd .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} correct = [mne.read_evokeds(file, condition="feedback-correct") for file in files] incorrect = [mne.read_evokeds(file, condition="feedback-incorrect") for file in files] mne.viz.plot_compare_evokeds({"correct": correct, "incorrect": incorrect}, picks="FCz"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](09-group_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=779 height=587} ::: ::: ::: {#0f4c46b7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} table = pd.DataFrame({"correct": [mean_amplitude(erp, "FCz", 0.2, 0.35) for erp in correct], "incorrect": [mean_amplitude(erp, "FCz", 0.2, 0.35) for erp in incorrect]}) table["difference"] = table["correct"] - table["incorrect"] print(table.round(1)) result = stats.ttest_rel(table["correct"], table["incorrect"]) print("t =", round(result.statistic, 2), " p =", round(result.pvalue, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` correct incorrect difference 0 3.2 1.9 1.3 1 6.2 5.0 1.2 2 0.4 0.6 -0.2 3 2.8 0.8 2.0 4 4.4 3.6 0.8 5 3.0 5.2 -2.2 6 0.5 2.6 -2.1 7 0.2 1.6 -1.4 8 -0.3 -0.3 -0.0 9 2.4 3.3 -0.8 t = -0.31 p = 0.767 ``` ::: ::: This time the differences go both ways, and the test finds nothing. The plot shows why. At about a quarter of a second the incorrect line does dip below the correct one, as in chapter 4. But straight after, it rises above. Our stretch of time spans both, and the two cancel in the mean. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Change both `0.35`s to `0.3`, so that the stretch ends before the lines cross, and run the cell again. What happens to the p-value? ::: If you tried that, you found the result changes from nothing to something. This is worth pausing on, because it is one of the main ways EEG research goes wrong. There are many reasonable electrodes and many reasonable stretches of time. Try enough of them after seeing the data and one will give a p-value under 0.05, whether or not the effect is real [@luck2017]. The honest position on what we have here: there is a dip at the expected place and time in the group average, the test on the stretch we chose beforehand does not support it, and a narrower stretch chosen *after looking* does. That is a hint, not a finding. Settling it would take a stretch of time fixed in advance from the literature, and more than ten participants. ## What a full analysis adds - **Choices fixed in advance.** Electrodes and time windows are taken from earlier studies, or written down before the data are examined. - **Tests over the whole time course.** There are methods that test every time point and electrode at once while accounting for the number of tests, so that no window has to be chosen. The most widely used is the cluster-based permutation test [@maris2007]. - **More participants.** Ten is small. With few participants only large and consistent effects, like stripe width, can be detected. ## Summary - One participant shows what can happen. A group shows what generally happens. - People's ERPs differ a lot. That variation is what a group test is measured against. - Reduce each participant to one number per condition, then compare across participants. The participants are the data points. - A choice of electrode or time window made after seeing the data cannot be trusted in the same way as one made before. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## In the lab's real pipeline Every analysis is run separately for each participant and each visit, and conclusions are drawn only from tests across participants. Where an effect is examined over time, the tests cover the whole time course with a correction for the number of time points, and the settings of each analysis are fixed in the script before it is run on the full dataset. :::
